subtopics.title: Audience analysis and interaction
subtopics.theory_md:
An oral presentation is a planned, purposeful talk to an audience. Before preparing, do **audience analysis**: who they are, what they know, why they are there, what they expect.

The audience's **attitude** decides interaction:
- **Favourable**: asks, comments, high interaction.
- **Neutral**: low unless prompted by questions or polls.
- **Hostile or sceptical**: challenges; handle calmly with evidence.
- **Indifferent**: bored, almost no interaction.
- **Shy or anxious**: silent even if interested.

Adjust level, tone and examples to the audience; open with a hook and invite questions.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of a shopkeeper. A regular customer chats, a stranger just browses, an angry customer argues. You change how you talk to each.
key_points: Audience analysis comes before content: who, why, what they know
Attitude types: favourable, neutral, hostile, indifferent, shy
Favourable audience gives high interaction; indifferent gives almost none
Presenter adapts level and tone, uses hooks and questions to draw interaction

questions.q: Audience analysis is done
options: only if there is a Q&A

questions.q: Which audience is most likely to interrupt and challenge the speaker?
questions.why: A sceptical audience argues; a shy one stays silent, a neutral one needs prompting.

questions.q: Name three audience attitudes and the interaction each produces.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Favourable**: interested, so many questions and comments.
2. **Neutral**: attends from duty, low interaction unless prompted.
3. **Hostile**: challenges, interaction high but confrontational.

(Indifferent and shy audiences also give little or no interaction.)

points: Attitude decides whether audience takes part or stays silent
Favourable: high interaction; neutral: low unless prompted
Hostile: challenging, presenter stays calm and uses evidence
Example and conclusion: analyse audience, hook, invite questions

subtopics.title: Planning and structuring a presentation
subtopics.theory_md:
Plan with purpose (inform, persuade, motivate), audience and time. Standard structure:

1. **Introduction**: hook, purpose statement, roadmap (about 10-15% of the time).
2. **Body**: 2-4 main points, each with an example or data.
3. **Conclusion**: summary of key ideas, closing line, invite questions.

Give times in an outline. A **book summary** names the book and author, then summarises: theme, main events or ideas, message, why you chose it. Speak at about 130 words per minute.
subtopics.basics_md: A talk is like a short journey: tell people where you are going, take them there, then remind them where you reached.
key_points: Three parts: introduction, body, conclusion
Introduction has hook, purpose and roadmap
Body points each backed by example or data
Outline shows timings; book summary gives title, author, summary, message

questions.q: The correct order of a presentation is
A 5-minute talk has an introduction of 45 seconds. What share of the time is that?
At 130 words per minute, how many words suit a 5-minute talk? Why speak from an outline rather than a script?
questions.model_answer_md:
$130 \times 5 = 650$ words.

An outline keeps the talk natural, lets you keep eye contact and adjust to the audience; a read-out script sounds flat and loses contact.
points: Outline gives eye contact and natural delivery
Introduction with hook, purpose, roadmap and timing
Body: why it matters, benefits, barriers with examples
Strategies: clear goals, roles, feedback, listening, tools
Conclusion: summary, closing line, invite questions; total 5 minutes with times shown
Name of the book and the author stated
Summary: background, key events, theme (about 300 words)

subtopics.title: Delivery and handling questions
subtopics.theory_md:
Good delivery: clear voice, moderate pace, pauses, **eye contact**, upright posture, natural gestures, no reading from slides. Rehearse and time it. Reduce nerves by preparing, breathing and arriving early.

**Handling questions**: listen fully, repeat or rephrase, answer briefly and honestly; if you do not know, say so and promise to find out. Stay calm with hostile questions. Close with a thank-you.
subtopics.basics_md: Speaking to a crowd is like talking to a friend, only more loudly and slowly.
key_points: Eye contact, posture, pace and pauses
Rehearse and time the talk
Listen, rephrase, answer briefly, admit when unsure
Stay calm with hostile questions

questions.q: The best response to a question you cannot answer is
options: admit it and offer to find out

questions.q: Which spoils delivery most?
questions.why: Reading slides breaks contact and bores the audience.

questions.q: List six points of good delivery in an oral presentation.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Clear, audible voice.
2. Moderate pace with pauses.
3. Eye contact with all sections.
4. Upright posture, natural gestures.
5. Speak from an outline, not read.
6. Keep to time and invite questions.

subtopics.title: Designing slides
subtopics.theory_md:
**Multimedia presentation**: a talk supported by text, images, charts, audio or video, usually through PowerPoint or Google Slides.

Slide rules:
- One idea per slide; **6 x 6 rule** (at most 6 bullets of 6 words).
- Large readable font (24 pt or more), high contrast, 2 fonts maximum.
- Visuals and charts over paragraphs; label graphs.
- Consistent template; limited animation.
- Title slide, outline, body, conclusion, references or Thank-you.

Slides support the speaker; they do not replace the speaker.
subtopics.basics_md: Slides are a signboard, not the speech. A signboard with a whole paragraph is not read by anyone.
key_points: One idea per slide, 6 x 6 rule
Readable font and strong contrast
Visuals and charts instead of long text
Consistent template, limited animation

questions.q: The 6 x 6 rule means at most
Which slide is best?
options: Three short bullets and a labelled chart

questions.q: State four guidelines for preparing effective slides.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. One idea per slide and the 6 x 6 rule.
2. Large font (24 pt or more) and high contrast.
3. Use labelled charts and images rather than paragraphs.
4. Consistent template and limited animation; check spelling.

subtopics.title: Using multimedia effectively
subtopics.theory_md:
**Advantages**: holds attention, explains complex data visually, retains memory, saves time. **Limitations**: technical failure, over-reliance on slides, distraction by effects, needs equipment.

Tips: carry a backup (pen drive, PDF); test the projector and sound before; stand beside, not behind, the screen; face the audience, not the slide; run a rehearsal with timing; use video or audio clips sparingly and short.
subtopics.basics_md: A good helper does not talk louder than you. Multimedia should help the message, not become it.
key_points: Advantages: attention, visual clarity, retention
Limitations: technical failure, distraction, over-reliance
Backup copy and pre-test of equipment
Face the audience, not the screen

questions.q: Give two advantages and two limitations of a multimedia presentation.
questions.model_answer_md:

**Limitations**: 1. technical failure; 2. speaker may depend on slides or be distracted by effects.

subtopics.title: Passive, aggressive, passive-aggressive, assertive
subtopics.theory_md:
The four styles:
- **Passive**: avoids conflict, does not state needs, says "it is okay". Others' rights come first.
- **Aggressive**: loud, blaming, dominating, ignores others. Own rights first.
- **Passive-aggressive**: seems calm but expresses anger indirectly (sarcasm, silent treatment, delay).
- **Assertive**: clear, honest, respectful; states needs and listens. Both parties' rights respected. Best style.

Assertive signs: steady voice, eye contact, "I" statements ("I feel ... when ..."), saying no politely.
subtopics.basics_md: A boy is asked to lend his notes though he needs them. Passive: lends and suffers. Aggressive: shouts "never". Passive-aggressive: lends a torn copy. Assertive: "I need them tonight, you can have them tomorrow."
key_points: Passive: avoids conflict, own needs ignored
Aggressive: dominates, blames, violates others
Passive-aggressive: indirect anger, sarcasm
Assertive: clear, honest, respectful; the best style

questions.q: Which style respects both your rights and the other person's?
questions.why: Assertive communication is honest and respectful.

questions.q: A student agrees to a group task with a smile but then deliberately submits it late. This is
questions.why: Anger is expressed indirectly, not stated.

questions.q: Differentiate passive, aggressive and assertive styles with one sentence each for the situation: a roommate plays loud music at night.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Passive**: says nothing and loses sleep.
**Aggressive**: shouts "You are so selfish, switch it off!"
**Assertive**: "I have an exam tomorrow; could you lower the volume after 10 pm?"

Assertive states the need clearly, politely and keeps the relationship.

subtopics.title: Formal and informal style, and choosing a style
subtopics.theory_md:
**Formal style**: official, impersonal, full sentences, no slang or contractions, titles and polite forms (reports, letters, interviews, presentations). **Informal style**: casual, personal, contractions and slang (friends, family, chats).

Choose style by **audience, purpose, context and relationship**. A senior at work needs a formal, assertive tone; a friend allows informal. Mixed-up register, such as slang in an application, makes a bad impression.
subtopics.basics_md: You wear different clothes to a wedding and to a cricket match. Language also dresses to the occasion.
key_points: Formal: impersonal, full forms, polite; informal: casual, slang
Choose by audience, purpose, context
Slang in a formal letter is an error of register

questions.q: Which is formal?
Which is the best style for a mail to a professor?
questions.why: Seniors and official matters need formal, clear writing.

questions.q: Rewrite formally: "Hey sir, can't come tomorrow, got fever, pls excuse."
questions.model_answer_md:
"Respected Sir, I am unable to attend class tomorrow as I am suffering from fever. I request you to kindly grant me leave for the day. Thanking you."

Full forms, polite opening, reason, request, closing.

subtopics.title: Voice modulation and its role
subtopics.theory_md:
**Voice modulation** is the controlled variation of **pitch** (high/low), **volume**, **pace**, **tone** and **pauses**, with stress and intonation, so speech is expressive, not monotonous.

Role:
1. Holds attention.
2. Shows emotion and attitude ("Come here" can be kind or angry).
3. Emphasises key words (*I* did not say that / I did not *say* that).
4. Improves clarity (pace, pauses).
5. Builds credibility in interviews and presentations.

Intonation: **rising** for yes/no questions, **falling** for statements and wh-questions.
subtopics.basics_md: A song with one note is boring. Your voice is the same: use high, low, loud, soft, fast, slow.
key_points: Elements: pitch, volume, pace, tone, pause, stress
Holds attention and conveys emotion
Stress changes meaning of a sentence
Rising tone for yes/no questions, falling for statements

questions.q: A flat, uniform voice is called
questions.why: Monotone has no variation in pitch or pace.

questions.q: Intonation of 'Are you coming?' is normally
questions.why: Yes/no questions rise at the end.

questions.q: Show with an example how stress changes the meaning of 'I did not say that.'
questions.model_answer_md:
Stress on **I**: someone else said it.
Stress on **not**: I definitely did not say it.
Stress on **say**: I implied it, did not say it.

So emphasis on a different word changes the meaning.

points: Definition: controlled variation of pitch, pace, volume, tone, pauses
Gives emphasis and meaning with example
Factors: pitch, volume, pace, pause, stress, tone, clarity
Examples: rise for question, fall for statement; pause before key point

subtopics.title: Pronunciation, sounds and minimal pairs
subtopics.theory_md:
**Pronunciation** is how sounds, stress and intonation are produced. It decides **intelligibility**.

A **phoneme** is the smallest sound that changes meaning. A **minimal pair** differs in one phoneme only: *ship* /ʃɪp/, *sheep* /ʃiːp/. Types: vowel length (/ɪ/ and /iː/: bit/beat), vowel quality (/æ/ and /ʌ/: cat/cut), voicing (/p/ and /b/: pat/bat), place or manner (/θ/ and /t/: thin/tin).

Wrong pronunciation changes the word (full/fool), stress (DEsert/deSERT), merges /v/ and /w/, or pronounces silent letters (debt, knife).
subtopics.basics_md: Change one sound and you change the word: cat becomes cut. That is why exact sounds matter.
key_points: Phoneme: smallest sound that changes meaning
Minimal pair differs in one sound only
Types: length, quality, voicing, place or manner
Wrong pronunciation reduces intelligibility

questions.q: Which is a minimal pair?
Pronouncing 'vest' as 'west' is an example of
Write five minimal pairs with transcription and a sentence for each.
questions.model_answer_md:
| Pair | Transcription | Sentence |
|---|---|---|
| bit / beat | /bɪt/, /biːt/ | A *bit* of practice helps *beat* the champion. |
| cat / cut | /kæt/, /kʌt/ | The *cat* got a *cut* on its paw. |
| pat / bat | /pæt/, /bæt/ | A *pat* on the back for holding the *bat*. |
| thin / tin | /θɪn/, /tɪn/ | A *thin* sheet of *tin*. |
| sip / zip | /sɪp/, /zɪp/ | *Sip* water, then *zip* the bag. |

Each pair differs in one phoneme.

points: Definition: pair differing in one sound with different meaning
Ten valid pairs, each with correct transcription
Role: intelligibility, clarity, credibility, saves effort
Wrong stress, consonant confusion, silent letters, intonation

subtopics.title: Word stress
subtopics.theory_md:
**Word stress** is extra force, length and pitch on one syllable of a word of two or more syllables: *TEACH-er*, *be-LIEVE*.

Importance: **intelligibility**, **meaning** (noun/verb), **rhythm and fluency**, listener comfort.

Rules of thumb:
- Two-syllable **nouns and adjectives**: first syllable (TEACHer, ENglish, SOMEthing).
- Two-syllable **verbs**: second syllable (beLIEVE, sugGEST, proVIDE, preSENT).
- Same spelling, noun first, verb second: PREsent/preSENT, REcord/reCORD, INcrease/inCREASE.
- Words with prefix like *per-, pro-, be-*: usually second (perHAPS, proPOSE).
subtopics.basics_md: Say 'present' as a gift and 'present' as to give. The first is PRE-sent, the second pre-SENT. Same letters, different stress.
key_points: Stress: force, length, pitch on one syllable
Nouns first syllable, verbs second syllable
Stress separates noun from verb (REcord/reCORD)
Importance: intelligibility, meaning, rhythm

questions.q: Stress in the noun 'increase' is on
questions.why: IN-crease as a noun; in-CREASE as a verb.

questions.q: Stress is on the second syllable in
questions.why: be-LIEVE; the others are stressed on the first.

questions.q: Mark stress (first or second syllable): doctor, forget, perhaps, therefore, record (verb).
questions.model_answer_md:
doctor: **first** (DOC-tor)
forget: **second** (for-GET)
perhaps: **second** (per-HAPS)
therefore: **first** (THERE-fore)
record (verb): **second** (re-CORD)

points: Definition: extra force, length and pitch on one syllable
Importance: intelligibility, noun/verb meaning, rhythm, listener comfort
Believe, suggest, provide, perhaps, present (verb), propose: second

subtopics.title: Purpose of GD and roles of participants
subtopics.theory_md:
A **group discussion (GD)** is a structured exchange of views by a group on a topic, usually 8-12 members for 15-20 minutes, used for selection.

**Purpose**: assess communication and personality together, observe reasoning and reaction to opposing views, test teamwork and leadership, reach consensus.

**Roles**: initiator (opens), leader/coordinator, information giver, opinion giver, clarifier, questioner/critic, peacemaker, summariser, gatekeeper/time keeper.
**Negative roles**: dominator, interrupter, aggressor, silent observer, off-topic speaker.

Opening confidently with facts and summarising at the end both score well.
subtopics.basics_md: A GD is a team game, not a debate to win. The examiner watches who helps the group move forward.
key_points: Purpose: selection, communication, personality, teamwork
Roles: initiator, leader, information giver, clarifier, peacemaker, summariser
Negative roles: dominator, interrupter, aggressor, silent
Positive contribution, not winning, is assessed

questions.q: State the purpose of a group discussion in four points.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Selection: assessing many candidates in a realistic setting.
2. Testing communication skills: clarity, listening, persuasion.
3. Observing personality: leadership, teamwork, confidence, emotional control.
4. Seeing how one reasons and reacts to opposing views.

points: Purpose: selection, communication skills, personality, reaction to opposition, sharing ideas
Positive roles: initiator, leader, information giver, opinion giver, clarifier, questioner, peacemaker, summariser, time keeper

subtopics.title: Personality traits assessed in a GD
subtopics.theory_md:
The panel judges the whole personality. Traits:
1. **Communication**: clarity, fluency, voice, language.
2. **Subject knowledge** and awareness.
3. **Listening**: refers to others' points.
4. **Leadership and initiative**.
5. **Team spirit**: no interruptions, gives chances.
6. **Confidence and body language**.
7. **Logical and analytical thinking**.
8. **Attitude and emotional control**.
9. **Flexibility and open-mindedness**.
10. **Creativity, time sense and relevance**.

Be assertive and balanced, neither silent nor aggressive.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine you are choosing a teammate for a project. You would want someone who knows things, speaks clearly, listens, and stays calm.
key_points: Communication, knowledge, listening
Leadership, team spirit, confidence

Flexibility, creativity, time sense

2. **Leadership**: starts, steers and summarises without dominating.
3. **Listening and team spirit**: builds on others' points, no interruption.

points: Whole personality assessed, not only knowledge
Communication, knowledge, listening, leadership, team spirit

subtopics.title: Grice's maxims in GD
subtopics.theory_md:
H. P. Grice's **Cooperative Principle**: make your contribution as required by the purpose of the talk. Four maxims:

| Maxim | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Quantity** | As informative as required, no more, no less |
| **Quality** | Be truthful; do not say what you lack evidence for |
| **Relation** | Be relevant to the topic |
| **Manner** | Be clear, brief, orderly, avoid ambiguity |

In GD: crisp points without monologue (Quantity); facts, not invented figures (Quality); link to the previous speaker (Relation); "two reasons: first ... second ..." (Manner).
subtopics.basics_md: Four rules of polite chat: say enough, say true, say relevant, say clearly.
key_points: Cooperative Principle by H. P. Grice
Quantity, Quality, Relation, Manner
Each applied to GD with a good and a poor example
Result: concise, credible, relevant, clear

2. **Quality**: "Our hostel survey shows most check messages in lectures" (real data).
3. **Relation**: "Building on Riya's point about distraction ...".
4. **Manner**: "Two reasons: distraction and cheating."

subtopics.title: Interview: preparation and types

subtopics.title: Structure of a paragraph
subtopics.theory_md:
A **paragraph** develops one idea. Parts:
1. **Topic sentence**: states the main idea.
2. **Supporting sentences**: reasons, examples, facts.
3. **Concluding sentence**: closes or links.

Qualities: **unity** (one idea), **coherence** (logical order, linkers like *moreover, however, therefore*), **completeness**, correct grammar, and the **word limit** (125 words is about 8-10 sentences; stay within 10 percent). Write it as one block, no bullets. Give the title only if asked.
subtopics.basics_md: A paragraph is a small room with one theme. Everything inside belongs to that theme.
key_points: One idea: unity
Topic sentence, supporting sentences, concluding sentence
Coherence with linkers
Stick to the word limit, one block, no bullets

For a '125-word paragraph' the best answer is

questions.model_answer_md:

subtopics.title: Opinion and topic paragraphs
subtopics.theory_md:
For a **statement or topic** ("Living in a hostel can be a learning experience"): topic sentence stating your stand; two or three reasons, each with a specific example; a concluding sentence.

For an **opinion** (agree/disagree): state the stand in line one, give reasons and a counter-point, end with a balanced conclusion. Use specific instances (ISRO satellites, Swachh Bharat). Positive and negative sides can both appear.

**Hostel life**: independence, tolerance, discipline, friendships, problem-solving; challenges like homesickness.
subtopics.basics_md: Say what you think, give two reasons with real examples, and close neatly.

subtopics.title: Format of a formal letter
subtopics.theory_md:
Parts, in order:
1. **Sender's address** (top right/left)
2. **Date**
3. **Receiver's address** (designation, institution)
4. **Subject line** (short, specific)
5. **Salutation**: Sir/Madam, Respected Sir/Madam, Dear Dr. Name
6. **Body**: opening (reference/purpose), details, request/closing
7. **Complimentary close**: Yours faithfully (name unknown), Yours sincerely (name known)
8. **Signature, name, designation**
9. **Enclosures**.

Style: formal, polite, concise, one purpose, no slang. Block format is preferred.
subtopics.basics_md: A letter is a form with fixed boxes. Fill each box in order and the reader knows where to look.

subtopics.title: Business letters: invitation, covering and change of arrangements
subtopics.theory_md:
**Business letter**: letterhead and reference number, date, inside address, subject, salutation, body, close, signature, enclosures.

- **Invitation**: event, date, venue, time, why this person, request to confirm by a date.
- **Covering letter** (conference/participants): welcome, event, themes (as a numbered list), enclosures, confirmation deadline.
- **Change of arrangements** (hotel manager): refer to the earlier confirmation, list changes as numbered points (rooms, hall, meals, dates), ask for a revised quotation by a date.

Use the "7 Cs": clear, concise, correct, courteous, complete, concrete, coherent.

subtopics.title: Functional resume and covering letter
subtopics.theory_md:
A **resume** (CV): short, one or two pages, for a particular job.

**Chronological** resume: by dates, newest first. **Covering (application) letter**: refers to the advertisement, highlights relevant qualifications and age/experience matching the advertisement, mentions the enclosed resume, requests an interview.

Invent details to match the advertisement (age, experience).

subtopics.title: Reports, memos and formats
subtopics.theory_md:
A **report** is a factual, objective, organised account of an event, situation or investigation, for a specific reader.

Format: **Title**, To/From/Date, **Introduction** (purpose), **Findings/Proceedings** (headed points), **Conclusion**, **Recommendations/Suggestions**, signature.

Formats:
- **Memorandum (memo)**: short internal document: To, From, Date, Subject, then body.
- **Letter report**: report in letter form to an outsider or authority.
- **Newsletter report**: with headline, byline, events described.

Style: past tense, impersonal, facts and figures, no opinions in findings.
subtopics.basics_md: A report answers: what happened or was found, what it means, what should be done.

subtopics.title: Describing charts and graphs
subtopics.theory_md:
Write 150 words in 3-4 paragraphs:
1. **Introduction**: what the chart shows (type, subject, unit).
2. **Main features**: highest and lowest, biggest difference, trends.
3. **Comparisons** with figures (percent, ratio, gap).
4. **Overall** summary.

Compute: gap = difference of two values; ratio = value1/value2; percentage change = (new - old)/old x 100. Always state units. Do not give opinions beyond the data; use language like *largest share*, *by contrast*, *whereas*, *almost equal*.
subtopics.basics_md: Describe what the picture shows, compare the big and small bars, and close with the overall message.

Linking words: by contrast, whereas, overall

subtopics.title: References and bibliography
subtopics.theory_md:
**References**: only the sources actually **cited** in the text, in a fixed style (APA, IEEE).
**Bibliography**: all sources **consulted**, cited or not, may include further reading.

Entry: author, year, title, publisher/journal, URL. In a report, sources appear at the end. Always acknowledge borrowed ideas to avoid plagiarism.
subtopics.basics_md: References are the people you quoted. A bibliography is everyone who helped you think.
key_points: References: cited sources only
Bibliography: all sources consulted
Entry: author, year, title, source
